note.question: How do learning agents affect understanding markets?
note.overview: Display advertising exchanges have largely shifted from second-price to first-price auctions, but the revenue and policy implications of this change remain contested. This paper studies a key mechanism often overlooked in this debate: that automated bidding agents typically optimize return on investment rather than standard profit and that they learn bidding strategies from repeated market feedback. In a benchmark model of display ad auctions, we show that this objective alone can make first-price auctions generate lower expected revenue than second-price auctions, even when bidders behave according to equilibrium and without algorithmic collusion.

models.summary: Display advertising exchanges have largely shifted from second-price to first-price auctions, but the revenue and policy implications of this change remain contested. This paper studies a key mechanism often overlooked in this debate: that automated bidding agents typically optimize return on investment rather than standard profit and that they learn bidding strategies from repeated market feedback. Simulations with common bandit-based bidding algorithms further show that agents lean toward these benchmark equilibria rather than systematically suppressing bids.
